title: Licensed boarding kennel blocks overheat in heatwave afternoons; licence expects 10–26°C but nobody sees the 3 pm peak
problem: Licence conditions and guidance under the 2018 animal-activity licensing regime expect kennel and cattery ambient temperature held roughly 10–26°C and dogs monitored for heat stress. In a heatwave, uninsulated blocks pass ~30°C mid-afternoon while staff are out walking dogs. A boarded dog dies of heatstroke, which brings an Animal Welfare Act prosecution (an unlicensed Cotswold boarder was fined ~£2,000 after a heatstroke death), owner compensation and vet bills, a star-rating downgrade at the next inspection (meaning a shorter licence and higher fees) and lost bookings.
who_suffers: Kennel/cattery staff, boarded dogs and cats, owners
buyer: Owner-operator / licence holder of a licensed boarding kennel or cattery (typically 20–100 pens)
industry: Licensed boarding kennels and catteries (England/Wales/Scotland)
sector: Animal care – kennels, catteries, vets, rescue
current_workaround: Min/max thermometer read once a day if at all; fans bought in a panic; staff judge heat by feel
sensor_concept: 2–4 battery LoRaWAN or LTE-M temperature/humidity sensors per block on one LTE gateway. Escalating phone alerts at ~25°C and ~28°C. An auto-generated daily min/max record in the format the council inspector asks for at star-rating inspections. Could be sold as an add-on by pet-business insurers.
notes: Strong c4 (licence conditions + inspections + star rating), c5 owner holds loss and budget, c8 trivial sensor; risks are c1 (per-dog claims ~£1–3k) and c7 (generic loggers), so pitch is licence-evidence not 'a logger'.

title: Kennel and cattery blocks catch fire at night with no staff on site and only a local smoke sounder
problem: Many licensed kennels have no one sleeping on site. Heated blocks with lamps, heat pads and old wiring catch fire overnight, and UK news repeatedly reports kennel fires killing 10+ dogs. Local sounders go unheard. Losses include the building rebuild (~£50k–£250k), compensation for boarded animals and licence suspension. Licence conditions require fire detection and an emergency plan, and insurers ask for it.
buyer: Owner / licence holder of a boarding kennel or cattery
industry: Licensed boarding kennels and catteries, rural sites without overnight staff
sector: Animal care – kennels, catteries, vets, rescue
current_workaround: Domestic smoke alarms, CCTV app on the owner's phone, occasionally an ARC-monitored alarm (~£300–£600/yr) at larger sites
sensor_concept: LTE-M rate-of-rise heat sensors (preferred over optical smoke in dusty, hairy blocks), mains-power-loss detection (heating off in winter) and a phone-call cascade to the owner and keyholders. Monthly self-test log for the licence inspector and insurer. Positioned as supplementary early warning, not an EN54 fire alarm.
notes: c1 large per incident and c4 (licensing + fire safety order + insurer) look strong; c7 risk from ARC monitoring, and the critic will need to see it is priced for commercial sites only.

title: Dogs overheat and die in heated cage dryers when groomers get distracted mid-session
problem: Groomers put washed dogs in heated cage or cabinet dryers and move on to the next dog. Brachycephalic, elderly or thick-coated dogs overheat within ~15–20 minutes. UK cases include Trudie the spaniel (Leicestershire, heard by magistrates) and Charlie the golden retriever, along with press campaigns for groomer licensing in Scotland and Wales. Costs are compensation, vet bills, insurer claims and loss of the salon's reputation.
buyer: Owner of a multi-groomer salon or grooming franchise (salon chains, mobile grooming franchises)
industry: Dog grooming salons and grooming franchises
sector: Animal care – kennels, catteries, vets, rescue
current_workaround: Kitchen timers, 'never leave unattended' policies; some salons have stopped heated cage drying altogether
sensor_concept: Clip-in temperature/humidity probe inside the cage plus a current clamp on the dryer heater, over BLE to a wall gateway (LTE-M). Buzzes the groomer's watch or phone after N minutes or above ~30°C, and auto-cuts power through a smart relay if no response. Per-dog drying-session log for insurer and complaint defence.
notes: c8 and c5 strong and c7 likely unserved; c1/c4 weaker (England has no groomer licensing yet), so pair with groomer insurers (c6) and the coming Scottish/Welsh regulation.

title: Dog day-care and dog-walker vans heat past 40°C while dogs wait between walks
problem: Licensed dog day-care businesses and professional walkers carry 6–12 dogs per van and leave some in the parked van between groups. In sun the van interior can pass ~40°C within ~20 minutes. Multiple UK cases of several dogs dying in a walker's van have led to prosecutions, compensation of ~£1–3k per dog, licence loss and the business closing. Day-care licence conditions cover welfare in transport.
buyer: Owner of a licensed dog day-care or dog-walking business running 2–10 vans
industry: Dog day care and professional dog walking (licensed in England since 2018 for day care)
sector: Animal care – kennels, catteries, vets, rescue
current_workaround: Dashboard thermometer, trust in drivers, occasional single-van GSM temperature alarms (~£150 + SIM) with no fleet view or records
sensor_concept: LTE-M van unit measuring cabin temperature at crate height, with 12V/ignition sense to know the engine is off and GPS. Alerts the driver and office when the engine is off and the van is above ~24°C or rising fast. Per-trip welfare log for the licence inspector and fleet view for the owner.
notes: c2 daily in summer, c5 owner, c8 cheap; c7 risk from consumer dog-van alarms, so gap is fleet records + licensing evidence; c1 depends on finding sourced deaths/prosecutions.

title: Aquatic and reptile shops lose whole stock systems overnight when power, a heater or the RCD trips
problem: Licensed pet shops selling fish and reptiles run centralised filtration and heated vivarium racks holding ~£10k–£50k of livestock. An overnight power cut, tripped RCD, failed heater/chiller or sump running dry kills whole systems by morning. Licence conditions require temperatures to be checked and recorded. Stock-deterioration insurance often expects an alarm or auto-dialler, and old diallers run on PSTN lines that are being switched off.
buyer: Owner of an independent aquatic/reptile retailer (OATA-member shop)
industry: Licensed pet shops with live fish/reptiles (aquatic centres, reptile shops)
sector: Animal care – kennels, catteries, vets, rescue
current_workaround: Staff read thermometers at opening; landline auto-diallers; hobbyist aquarium controllers per tank
sensor_concept: LTE-M hub with battery backup that detects mains loss, plus waterproof temperature probes in 2–4 sumps/vivarium racks and a float switch for sump low level. Alerts to the owner. Daily auto-log for the licence inspector and insurer.
notes: c1 stock losses and c4 (pet-selling licence + insurer alarm condition) look good, c6 via aquatic wholesaler reps/OATA; c7 risk from Wi-Fi hobby controllers (Apex/GHL) not built for shop-wide records.

title: Licensed dog breeders lose whole litters to chilling or overheating in the first fortnight
problem: Licensed breeders (England: 3+ litters/year) whelp litters worth ~£10k–£25k (e.g. 8 pups × £1.5–3k). Newborn puppies can't regulate their own temperature. A failed heat pad or lamp at 3 am chills the litter, an over-hot lamp causes heatstroke, and heat lamps start fires. Licence conditions expect suitable, monitored whelping temperatures, and puppy deaths lead to complaints and inspection findings.
who_suffers: Breeders (sleeping next to the whelping box), puppies
buyer: Licensed dog breeder (owner-operator)
industry: Licensed dog breeding establishments
sector: Animal care – kennels, catteries, vets, rescue
current_workaround: Breeder sleeps by the box, baby monitors, stick-on thermometers
sensor_concept: Bedding-level temperature probe plus a current clamp on the heat lamp/pad, on LTE-M (no Wi-Fi needed in outbuildings). Alerts on out-of-band temperature or heater failure. Whelping log for the licence inspector and puppy buyers.
notes: c1 litter value and c5 owner are strong and c8 is simple; c6 weak (breeder insurers / Kennel Club Assured Breeders) and c7 risk of consumer thermometers.

title: Farm and equine vets' car-boot medicines cook in summer and freeze in winter with no records
problem: Farm and equine vets carry ~£2k–£8k of medicines and vaccines in car boots every day. Boots pass ~40°C in summer and freeze in winter. VMD rules and the RCVS Practice Standards Scheme expect medicines in vehicles stored to label and monitored. An excursion means discarding stock or using a compromised vaccine, which risks a disease breakdown and a client complaint.
buyer: Practice manager / clinical director of a farm or equine practice, or compliance lead at a corporate vet group
industry: Farm and equine veterinary practices (ambulatory vehicles)
sector: Animal care – kennels, catteries, vets, rescue
current_workaround: Max/min thermometers in boots that nobody resets; cool boxes; refrigerated boot units in some vehicles
sensor_concept: BLE/LTE-M temperature logger in the drug box (and fridge drawer where fitted). Alerts the vet's phone at ~25°C/~30°C and keeps an automatic daily record per vehicle for PSS/VMD inspection.
notes: c4 (PSS/VMD record duty) and c5 (practice manager budget) look good, c6 via vet wholesalers (Covetrus/NVS) who deliver daily; c7 risk from generic transport loggers.

title: Boarding kennels and day care served noise abatement notices with no objective barking record
problem: Kennels and dog day care in semi-rural areas draw neighbour complaints about barking. Councils serve statutory-nuisance abatement notices (EPA 1990 s80), and planning conditions cap noise. Breach leads to prosecution (fines for business premises in England/Wales are uncapped) and blocks planning permission to expand. The owner has no objective data to rebut neighbours' diaries, and paid acoustic surveys cost ~£1–3k each.
buyer: Owner / licence holder of a boarding kennel or day-care site
industry: Boarding kennels and dog day-care centres near housing
sector: Animal care – kennels, catteries, vets, rescue
current_workaround: Neighbour diaries versus the owner's word; occasional paid acoustic consultant surveys
sensor_concept: MEMS sound-level sensors (dBA LAeq/LAmax only, no audio stored) inside blocks and at the boundary, battery/solar LTE-M. Alerts staff to sustained barking so they can intervene, plus a monthly report against planning-condition limits for the EHO.
notes: c2 daily, c3 paid consultant surveys, c4 statutory nuisance + planning conditions, c8 cheap; risk that non-calibrated data is not evidential, and c7 (Airbnb noise monitors are a different niche).

title: Pet crematoria's freezers at vet practices fail or overflow between weekly collections
problem: Pet crematoria and aftercare firms place chest freezers in vet practices to hold deceased pets and collect on fixed weekly rounds. A freezer fails or overfills between visits and bodies decompose, leaving distraught owners and practice complaints that cost the crematorium the contract. Other collection runs find the freezer nearly empty and waste the trip.
who_suffers: Practice staff, grieving owners, crematorium drivers
buyer: Operations director of a pet crematorium / aftercare company serving 50–500 practices
industry: Pet cremation and aftercare services to veterinary practices
sector: Animal care – kennels, catteries, vets, rescue
current_workaround: Fixed weekly rounds; practice phones when full or when the freezer is warm
sensor_concept: LTE-M unit per freezer with temperature probe, lid-open counter and load-cell feet for fill level. Alerts the crematorium on failure or near-full and drives route planning.
notes: c5 a service firm that bills per collection, c6 it already visits weekly, c9 per-freezer subscription; risks c1 (reputational loss, not £) and c7 (freezer alarms are generic).

title: Multi-branch community pharmacies breach 'store below 25°C' in heatwaves with no weekend data
problem: Most medicines are labelled 'store below 25°C'. Older dispensaries and back stockrooms, especially those facing south or without A/C, pass 25°C in heatwaves. GPhC standards expect storage to be monitored, but most branches read a min/max thermometer once a day and have no weekend data. A sustained excursion should trigger a stock assessment for a dispensary holding ~£30k–£80k of stock, and superintendents have no view across branches.
buyer: Superintendent pharmacist / head of operations at an independent pharmacy multiple (5–50 branches)
industry: Community pharmacy multiples
current_workaround: Daily min/max reading on paper; plug-in fans; excursions quietly ignored
sensor_concept: Two battery ambient sensors per branch (dispensary and stockroom) on LoRaWAN/LTE-M, with alerts and a head-office dashboard showing every branch. GPhC-ready records, and it can share a gateway with fridge probes.
notes: c4 (GPhC standards/inspections) and c5 (superintendent budget) look good, c6 via buying groups/wholesalers; c7 risk since fridge-logger vendors also sell ambient sensors.

title: Care home medicine rooms exceed 25°C and CQC marks the home down for missing temperature records
problem: CQC inspections repeatedly cite care homes whose medicines rooms ran above the recommended temperature or had no daily records. Examples include a Scunthorpe home downgraded to 'Requires improvement' with no room temperature monitoring, a Fenland home with only three days of readings in a month, and the Ramping Cat breach. A lower rating hits fees, occupancy and council contracts. Small unventilated treatment rooms peak in summer.
buyer: Registered manager / regional operations manager of a care home group; sold through the home's supplying pharmacy
industry: Care home medicines storage, supplied by community pharmacies
current_workaround: Twice-daily paper charts, portable A/C units bought after an inspection
sensor_concept: LTE-M or LoRaWAN temperature sensor in each medicines room and trolley bay, giving an automatic record and alerts. The supplying pharmacy's care-home team reviews the data remotely during its medicines audits.
notes: c4 and c10 are strong (CQC enforcement + local press), c6 via the supplying pharmacy that already visits; risk c1 (rating harm is hard to put in £) and c7 (generic loggers).

title: Pharmacy controlled-drug cabinets left unlocked or opened out of hours with no audit trail
problem: Schedule 2 CDs must be kept in a locked cabinet under the Safe Custody Regulations. In busy sessions cabinets stand open with keys in the lock. Staff diversion of opioids and gabapentinoids only surfaces when the running balance is off, and night-time burglaries target CD cabinets. GPhC and police CD liaison officer inspections follow, with stock losses, investigations and fitness-to-practise cases.
buyer: Superintendent pharmacist / governance lead at a pharmacy multiple or dispensing GP practice
industry: Community pharmacies and dispensing doctor practices
current_workaround: Weekly running-balance checks; CCTV review after a discrepancy; key held by the RP
sensor_concept: Reed switch plus accelerometer on the CD cabinet door (opening, forced-entry tamper), on LTE-M. Alerts when the door is open more than N minutes or opened out of hours, and the open/close log is reconciled against CD register entries.
notes: c4 statutory safe custody and c8 trivial; c7 likely unserved; c1 is the risk because diversion losses need sourced figures (court cases of pharmacy staff theft).

title: On-farm livestock vaccines stored in domestic fridges that freeze in winter sheds
problem: Farmers keep ~£1k–£5k of livestock vaccines (clostridial, BVD, lepto, pneumonia) in old domestic fridges in sheds and dairies. Fridges in unheated buildings freeze the contents in winter and warm up in summer. Frozen vaccine fails silently, and the herd breakdown is blamed on the vaccine or the vet. Red Tractor and VMD rules require medicines stored to label.
buyer: Farm vet practice (sells vaccines and herd-health plans) or agricultural merchant SQP manager, bundled into the health-plan fee
industry: On-farm veterinary medicine storage (cattle/sheep units)
current_workaround: Domestic fridge thermometer or nothing; vet asks at the annual health-plan review
sensor_concept: LTE-M fridge probe in a glycol buffer bottle (rural sites have no Wi-Fi). Alerts the farmer and vet, and keeps a record for Red Tractor audit.
notes: c4 Red Tractor/VMD and c6 farm vets visit monthly; the generic fridge-logger c7 flag applies, so this rural LTE-M farm sub-niche must be shown to be unserved.

title: Online pharmacies can't prove the cold chain when GLP-1 weight-loss pens arrive warm
problem: Online pharmacies dispatch large volumes of weight-loss injection pens (fridge lines before first use) in insulated packs by courier. Failed or delayed deliveries in hot weather sit in depots for 24–48 h. Patients report warm packs and the pharmacy replaces pens worth ~£150–£300 each, or the pens are used compromised. GPhC has tightened standards for online pharmacies, and nobody can prove the transit temperature either way.
buyer: Head of operations / superintendent pharmacist at a high-volume online pharmacy
industry: Online/distance-selling pharmacies dispatching fridge lines
current_workaround: Insulated boxes with ice packs sized for ~48 h; single-use indicator labels on some; replacing on request
sensor_concept: Reusable BLE/NFC temperature tag in each pack, or an LTE-M tracker in a sample of parcels per route to profile courier performance. Evidence for replacement disputes and for choosing couriers.
notes: c2 daily volume and c5 clear; risks c7 (cheap indicator labels already exist) and c8 (cost per parcel), so it may only work as route sampling.

title: Homecare patients' domestic fridges freeze or warm high-cost biologics and nobody knows until a replacement is ordered
problem: Homecare providers deliver high-cost biologics and other fridge medicines (~£300–£1,500 per pack) to patients' homes. Domestic fridges freeze items at the back or fail, and packs get left on the side. Replacements are funded by the NHS/provider, and provider QA cannot evidence storage after delivery.
who_suffers: Patients, homecare nurses, provider QA teams
buyer: Quality / operations director at a homecare medicines provider
industry: Clinical homecare medicines services
current_workaround: Patient education leaflets, phone check-ins, replace when a patient reports a problem
sensor_concept: Small LTE-M (no patient Wi-Fi) fridge puck shipped with the first delivery. Alerts the provider on out-of-range temperature and gives an excursion record to support or refuse replacement.
notes: c1 high item value and c2 continuous; c5 enterprise buyer and patient homes make c6/c8 harder; c7 probably unserved.

title: Medical cannabis pharmacies' Schedule 2 flower stock dries out or moulds with humidity drift
problem: Specialist pharmacies dispensing Schedule 2 medical cannabis flower hold ~£100k+ of stock in CD-compliant storage. Humidity drift dries the flower or lets mould grow, and microbial contamination has led to product recalls. Combined with CD safe-custody and theft risk, a ruined batch is a large write-off and a GPhC/Home Office issue.
buyer: Superintendent pharmacist at a specialist medical cannabis pharmacy
industry: UK specialist medical cannabis dispensing pharmacies
current_workaround: Hygrometers read by hand, humidity packs, CCTV
sensor_concept: Temperature/RH sensors in each storage unit plus a vault-door reed switch, on LTE-M. Alerts and an audit record.
notes: c1 stock value, c5 clear, c7 unserved, c8 simple; c6 weak and the market is small (a few dozen pharmacies).

title: Independent clinical-trial sites log investigational medicine temperatures by hand, so weekend excursions quarantine stock
problem: Commercial research sites and GP research practices must store investigational medicinal products under continuous temperature control with records reviewed by the sponsor. Manual daily readings miss weekend excursions, so sponsors quarantine kits (often thousands of £) and log protocol deviations, and MHRA GCP inspections cite poor storage records.
buyer: Site director / operations lead at an independent research site network
industry: Independent clinical research sites and GP research practices
current_workaround: Daily min/max readings on paper; sponsor-supplied loggers for some studies
sensor_concept: LTE-M ambient and fridge sensors per IMP store, giving per-study reports in sponsor format with alerts.
notes: c4 GCP/sponsor contracts strong, c5 site director; c7 risk from generic monitoring vendors in pharma.

title: Waste-wood, green-waste and SRF stockpiles self-heat between twice-daily probe rounds and burn the site
problem: Environment Agency Fire Prevention Plan guidance requires temperature monitoring on piles stored for 3 months or more (per letsrecycle), and permitted sites commit in their FPPs to twice-daily probe or thermal-gun readings. Readings get skipped at weekends and handheld IR only sees the surface. Deep-seated self-heating becomes a fire costing ~£100k–£m, with EA enforcement, permit suspension, insurer exclusions and punitive premiums.
buyer: Site manager / operations director of an independent permitted waste-wood, green-waste or recycling site
industry: Permitted waste transfer/treatment sites storing combustible waste
current_workaround: Manual lance thermometers twice daily, IR guns, fixed thermal cameras (~£20k–£60k) only at large sites
sensor_concept: Rugged steel lances with 2–3 thermistors at 1–2 m depth and a LoRaWAN head, left in piles. Solar LTE gateway. Alerts above ~50°C or on a rising trend, plus an automatic FPP monitoring log for the EA officer and insurer surveyor.
notes: c1/c4/c10 strong (EA FPP + enforcement + fire news), c2 twice daily, c3 labour; c7 gap versus enterprise thermal cameras; c8 risk that loaders damage lances, and RDF bales should not be probed.

title: Composting sites hand-probe windrows daily to prove sanitisation, and missing readings fail the batch
problem: Composting sites under the Animal By-Products Regulations or PAS 100 and the Compost Quality Protocol must prove each batch held sanitisation temperatures (time-temperature criteria) with records. Staff push handheld probes into windrows daily and write the readings down. Missing or low readings mean the batch must be re-processed or cannot leave waste status, and certification audits fail.
buyer: Site manager / owner of an independent or farm-based composting site
industry: Open-windrow and in-vessel composting sites (ABPR / PAS 100)
current_workaround: Daily manual probing with paper/spreadsheet logs; some sites buy imported wireless probes (~$1k+ each)
sensor_concept: Wireless multi-depth compost lances on LoRaWAN, tracking time-temperature compliance per batch automatically. Alerts on stalled heating and exports certification records.
notes: c2 daily, c3 labour, c4 ABPR/PAS 100 record duty, c9 records per batch; c7 gap is price versus imported probes; c1 needs sourced batch-failure costs.

title: Skip lamps go out or get stolen overnight, but the skip firm carries the Highways Act lighting duty
problem: Section 139 of the Highways Act makes the skip owner light a skip on the highway through the hours of darkness, with a level-3 fine on conviction. Council permits require amber lamps on each corner, lit all night. Lamps are stolen or their batteries die, cyclists and motorcyclists hit unlit skips and claims follow, and permit overstays draw council fines. A skip firm with hundreds of skips out cannot see any of it.
who_suffers: Skip-hire drivers and office staff, road users
buyer: Owner / transport manager of a skip-hire company (100–2,000 skips)
industry: Skip hire on the public highway
current_workaround: Drivers drop lamps with the skip, customers are told to look after them, and nobody checks
sensor_concept: Clip-on unit with a photodiode aimed at a lamp, tilt sensor and GPS, on LTE-M. At dusk it confirms the lamps are flashing and alerts the depot if not. A nightly compliance log, and GPS proves permit location and days on site.
notes: c2 nightly, c4 statutory duty + permit conditions, c5 owner, c7 unserved, c8 cheap; c1 depends on sourcing unlit-skip injury claims.

title: Retail battery take-back tubs overfill with lithium cells and self-heat before the scheme collects
problem: Retailers selling portable batteries must offer take-back under the Waste Batteries Regulations 2009, and compliance schemes collect the tubs. Damaged lithium cells self-heat in tubs in stockrooms, and full tubs push batteries into general waste, where they start bin-lorry fires. Collections are either too late (overflow) or wasted trips.
buyer: Operations manager of a battery compliance scheme or its collection contractor
industry: Retail battery take-back collection networks
current_workaround: Store requests a collection online when it remembers; fixed-interval collections
sensor_concept: Load-cell base plus thermistor under the tub, on NB-IoT/LTE-M. Fill (kg) and temperature-rise alerts that drive collection routing.
notes: c5 service firm billing per collection, c6 its collectors visit, c7 unserved; c1/c4 need sourced store-fire incidents.

title: Landfill leachate wells dipped by hand every month to meet permit limits
problem: Operational and closed landfills under EA permits must monitor leachate levels in dozens of wells (often monthly) against compliance limits. Technicians drive out to dip each well by hand. Pump failures between visits breach leachate-head limits, which brings EA compliance scores and enforcement.
buyer: Landfill aftercare / environmental manager at a waste company, or the consultancy contracted to monitor
industry: Permitted operational and closed landfill sites
current_workaround: Monthly manual dip-meter rounds; expensive telemetry loggers at a few key wells
sensor_concept: Submersible pressure transducer plus a LoRaWAN head on the well cap, reporting level daily, with alerts for pump failure and rising head.
notes: c2 monthly duty, c3 labour, c4 permit; risks c8 (transducer in leachate, ~£100+) and c5 (council/enterprise owners).

title: Retail cardboard balers misused with interlocks defeated, while bale collections run blind
problem: Supermarkets and retailers rent vertical balers from baler firms that service them (PUWER/LOLER) and collect bales for rebate. HSE prohibits under-18s from using balers, and there are prosecutions after amputations where interlocks were defeated. Meanwhile bales pile up and block fire exits, or trucks arrive to collect two bales.
who_suffers: Store staff, baler-firm engineers and drivers
buyer: Operations director of a baler rental/service and bale-collection company
industry: Retail back-of-store vertical balers and compactors
current_workaround: 6-monthly service visits, fixed collection rounds, store phones when full
sensor_concept: Current clamp on the baler motor plus a reed switch on the chamber door, on LTE-M. Counts bales ejected and flags the motor running with the door open (interlock defeat). Collection routing and a safety-incident log.
notes: c5/c6 strong (service firm already visits), c8 simple; c1/c4 need sourced HSE baler prosecutions, and c7 must check OEM telematics.

title: Thieves empty restaurants' used-cooking-oil drums before the licensed collector arrives
problem: Used cooking oil is valuable biodiesel feedstock that collectors buy from restaurants. Organised thieves empty UCO drums and tanks behind restaurants before the licensed collector's visit, and other visits find half-empty containers. Waste duty-of-care and sustainability traceability (ISCC/RTFO) break down when oil goes missing.
buyer: Operations director of a UCO collection company
industry: Used cooking oil collection from food outlets
current_workaround: Fixed-frequency rounds, padlocks on drums, restaurant phones when full
sensor_concept: Ultrasonic or load-cell level sensor plus lid-open/tilt sensor in collector-supplied containers, on LTE-M. Theft alert if the level drops with no scheduled collection, and routing by fill level.
notes: c5 service firm, c6 it visits, c7 likely unserved; c1 per site is small but per collector per year may be large, and the critic will need sourced theft figures.

title: Licensed asbestos contractors' waste skips left unlocked overnight on occupied sites
problem: Licensed asbestos removal contractors must keep bagged asbestos waste secure in lockable skips or containers until consignment (CAR 2012, HSE licensing). Skips left unlocked at shift end are opened by scavengers, children or fly-tippers, which brings HSE enforcement, licence review at renewal and client contract loss.
buyer: Contracts manager / director of an HSE-licensed asbestos removal contractor
industry: Licensed asbestos removal (HSE licence holders)
current_workaround: Padlocks, supervisor end-of-shift checklist and photos
sensor_concept: Reed switch on the skip lid/door plus tilt sensor, on LTE-M. Alerts if opened out of hours or left unlocked at shift end, and a daily lock log for HSE licence assessment and the client.
notes: c4 strong (CAR 2012 + licensing), c5 director, c7 unserved, c8 trivial; c1/c2 need sourced enforcement cases.

title: Stocking-finance lenders pay auditors to count financed cars, and sold-out-of-trust stock still slips through
problem: Lenders funding dealer stock (floorplan / stocking finance) send auditors (SGS, RGIS, DEKRA) to physically verify each funded car. RGIS describes one auditor per ~100 vehicles. Between periodic or unannounced audits a dealer can sell a funded car and keep the cash for weeks, and when a dealer fails the lender loses six figures.
who_suffers: Lender credit/risk teams, auditors, honest dealers inconvenienced by audits
buyer: Head of dealer risk / credit at a stocking-finance lender or OEM captive finance arm
industry: UK car-dealer stocking finance (floorplan)
sector: Motor trade – garages, dealerships, vehicle storage
current_workaround: Periodic physical audits by SGS/RGIS/DEKRA; photo-app 'digital audits' (e.g. SBS)
sensor_concept: BLE tag (windscreen sticker or key-fob) on each funded vehicle plus an LTE gateway at the dealer site. Daily presence report per VIN, with an alert if a funded car is absent more than ~24 h without settlement. Physical audits are kept for exceptions only.
notes: c3 paid audits quantified, c5 lender risk head owns loss + budget, c6 audit firms as channel, c2 continuous; c7 needs UK gap evidence (US GPS lot-check exists), c1 needs sourced dealer-fraud losses.

title: Motor trade insurers dispute theft claims when dealers can't prove keys were locked in the safe overnight
problem: Motor trade policies commonly require all vehicle keys to be in a locked safe while premises are unattended. Key burglaries and keyless thefts from forecourts (~£15k–£60k per car) lead to disputes when the dealer can't prove the keys were locked away, and FOS decisions show key-custody arguments decide motor theft claims. Small dealers carry the loss.
buyer: Owner of an independent used-car dealer / motor trader
industry: Independent used-car dealers and motor traders
sector: Motor trade – garages, dealerships, vehicle storage
current_workaround: Honour system; key cabinets with paper logbooks; costly electronic key systems (Traka/KeyTracker) only at franchised dealers
sensor_concept: Reed and bolt-throw switch on the key safe, optional BLE key-tag count, on LTE-M. Timestamped locked/unlocked log, an alert if the safe is open after close of business, and a report for insurer claims.
notes: c4 insurer warranty, c5 owner, c6 via motor trade brokers/insurers, c8 trivial; c1/c10 depend on sourced trade claim refusals.

title: Crash-damaged EVs in recovery and salvage yards reignite days later and burn neighbouring stock
problem: Recovery operators, salvage agents and bodyshops take in crash-damaged EVs and PHEVs. UK guidance (DfT summary) says to quarantine them outdoors 15 m from anything and monitor for up to 48 h, but batteries can reignite days or weeks later. One fire can spread through a yard of salvage stock (~£100k+). Insurers and police recovery contracts increasingly specify quarantine, and yards rely on someone walking past.
who_suffers: Yard staff, fire service, neighbouring businesses
buyer: Owner / yard manager of a vehicle recovery and storage operator (police VRS contractor, salvage agent) or bodyshop manager
industry: Vehicle recovery compounds, salvage yards and accident-repair centres
sector: Motor trade – garages, dealerships, vehicle storage
current_workaround: Quarantine bay with periodic visual checks, IR guns, fixed thermal cameras only at large salvage sites
sensor_concept: 2–3 magnetic temperature pucks under the battery tray and one in the cabin, on LTE-M. Alerts above ~45°C or on a rising slope, with a 48–72 h quarantine log per vehicle for insurers and the fire service. Pucks reused vehicle to vehicle.
notes: c1 yard-fire losses, c4 DfT/insurer guidance, c5 owner-operator, c8 cheap; c2 depends on EV intake rate, and c7 versus thermal cameras.

title: Two-post vehicle lifts raise unevenly or drop when an arm slips, and daily pre-use checks are never written down
problem: Cars fall from two-post lifts when arms slip or carriages rise unevenly, crushing mechanics. HSE prosecutes garages after these incidents (fines ~£k–£100k+). LOLER requires thorough examination every 6 months and PUWER expects pre-use checks, but those are rarely documented.
buyer: Garage owner / aftersales manager at a dealer group
industry: Independent garages and franchised dealer workshops
sector: Motor trade – garages, dealerships, vehicle storage
current_workaround: Paper pre-use checklist (often blank); LOLER exam by an insurer engineer or the lift service firm
sensor_concept: Accelerometer/tilt module on each carriage plus a current clamp on the lift motor. Detects uneven raise, sudden drop and overload-like current, and counts cycles. BLE to a workshop LTE gateway, with an automatic daily-use log and data for the LOLER examiner.
notes: c4 LOLER/PUWER + HSE prosecutions, c6 lift service firms and insurer engineers, c8 cheap; c7 needs to show retrofit is unserved, since OEMs add telemetry only to new lifts.

title: Stored stock cars go flat: 12V batteries die on forecourts and in compounds, breaking OEM storage rules
problem: New and used cars stored for weeks on forecourts, overflow lots and logistics compounds drain their 12V batteries (connected-car modules). Flat batteries mean jump-starts, replacement batteries (~£100–£300), delayed handovers and EVs that can't be moved. OEM storage manuals require periodic battery checks or charging, and deep-discharge damage can void battery warranty claims.
who_suffers: PDI technicians, sales staff, compound operatives
buyer: Stock / PDI manager at a dealer group, or operations manager at a vehicle logistics / storage compound
industry: Dealer stock storage and vehicle logistics compounds
sector: Motor trade – garages, dealerships, vehicle storage
current_workaround: Weekly walk-round with a battery tester; trickle chargers on some stock
sensor_concept: OBD-II plug-in dongle reading battery voltage (BLE to a site gateway, or LTE-M), fitted at intake. Alert below ~12.2 V, plus a log of OEM storage compliance and the car's location in the compound.
notes: c2 weekly, c3 labour, c4 OEM storage requirements, c8 trivial; c1 per incident is small (aggregate case), and c7 versus OBD telematics.

title: Airport meet-and-greet parkers can't prove customers' cars weren't driven while in their custody
problem: Meet-and-greet operators hold customers' cars for 1–3 weeks. News and consumer-group reports keep showing cars joyridden, parked in fields or caught speeding. Customers claim damage and extra mileage, airports ban rogue operators, and honest operators can't prove a car stayed put.
buyer: Owner / operations manager of a meet-and-greet parking company (BPA-approved / Park Mark)
industry: Airport meet-and-greet and valet parking
sector: Motor trade – garages, dealerships, vehicle storage
current_workaround: Odometer photos at handover, CCTV at the compound
sensor_concept: GPS plus accelerometer tag (LTE-M) placed in the car at handover. Motion log shows only valet moves, with a geofence alert and a 'parked and untouched' report sent to the customer.
notes: c5 owner, c8 cheap, c10 news/consumer complaints; c4 weak (no duty) and c6 unclear.

title: Dealers storing battery-fire recall vehicles outdoors for weeks while awaiting parts
problem: Battery-fire recalls on some PHEVs/EVs tell owners not to charge and to park outdoors. Dealers end up holding recalled vehicles awaiting parts for weeks or months, and OEMs ask for outdoor storage and checks. A fire in a dealer compound spreads to stock and the building.
buyer: Aftersales manager / dealer principal (potentially funded via the OEM recall programme)
industry: Franchised dealers holding recall-affected PHEVs/EVs
sector: Motor trade – garages, dealerships, vehicle storage
current_workaround: Park at the far end of the lot; visual checks
sensor_concept: Magnetic temperature pucks on battery trays plus a yard gateway (LTE-M). Alerts, and recall-storage evidence for the OEM.
notes: c4 OEM instructions and c5 dealer; c2 is episodic (depends on recalls), so it may be weaker than the recovery-yard version.

title: Commercial tyre fitters inflate split-rim and truck tyres outside the cage when busy, and explosions kill fitters
problem: Inflating truck and split-rim tyres outside a restraining cage or without remote inflation risks rim/bead explosions that kill or maim fitters. HSE guidance requires cages or remote inflation, and HSE has prosecuted tyre firms after deaths with large fines. Fitters bypass the cage when rushed in depots or at the roadside.
buyer: Operations / SHEQ director of a commercial tyre service company
industry: Commercial vehicle tyre depots and mobile truck tyre fitting
sector: Motor trade – garages, dealerships, vehicle storage
current_workaround: Training, cages provided, supervisor spot checks
sensor_concept: Pressure/flow switch on the inflation line plus a reed switch on the cage door (or BLE proximity of the chuck in the cage), on LTE-M. Alerts and logs any inflation above the threshold while the cage is open.
notes: c1/c4 HSE prosecutions, c5 SHEQ director; c8 risk in mobile-van installation, c7 to check.

title: Holiday cottages on private water supplies drink untreated water when the UV lamp quietly fails
problem: Holiday lets and parks on boreholes or springs are 'commercial' private water supplies under the Private Water Supplies Regulations, with council risk assessments and sampling. DWI case studies show holiday-cottage UV units not disinfecting (starter never checked, lamps not serviced), leading to E. coli and Regulation 18 notices that restrict the supply and require written maintenance procedures and monitoring of the disinfection unit. Guest illness means refunds, claims and lost bookings.
buyer: Owner-operator of holiday cottages / holiday park on a private supply
industry: Self-catering holiday lets and parks on private water supplies
current_workaround: Annual service by a water-treatment engineer; owner glances at the UV unit's local LED; council samples annually
sensor_concept: Current clamp on the UV lamp ballast plus a UV-C photodiode on the sight-glass port and a pulse flow meter, on LTE-M. Alerts the owner and service engineer on lamp failure, low UV or water flowing with the lamp off, and keeps a monitoring log that satisfies notice requirements.
notes: c4 strong (PWS Regs + Reg 18 notices requiring monitoring), c6 water-treatment engineers already service the units, c8 simple; c1 needs sourced outbreak costs.

title: Spa hotel laundry: oily massage towels self-heat after tumble drying and set the laundry room on fire overnight
problem: Massage-oil residue that survives a low-temperature wash self-heats once dried towels are stacked or bagged. London Fire Brigade attributed a South Kensington hotel laundry fire to oily spa robes and towels in a dryer, and an Islington spa blaze to oil-soaked towels. A Cornwall bag of towels spontaneously combusted, and fire services issue repeated warnings. Hotel fire losses run £100k+ along with closure, and insurers expect cool-down cycles and safe stacking.
buyer: General manager / head of housekeeping / spa director at a spa hotel or day spa
industry: Spa hotels and day spas with on-site laundries
current_workaround: Fire-service advice posters, hot washes, 'don't stack warm towels' rules, dryers stopped early when busy
sensor_concept: Temperature probes in laundry trolleys/stacking shelves plus a current clamp on each dryer to verify the cool-down phase ran, on LoRaWAN/LTE-M. Alerts on a rising stack temperature at night, with a nightly log for the insurer.
notes: c1/c10 strong (multiple LFB incidents + fire-service warnings), c8 simple, c7 likely unserved; c6 via commercial laundry equipment service firms, and c4 needs insurer wording.

title: B&Bs and small hotels leave the fire alarm panel in fault for weeks and skip the weekly test log
problem: Guest houses, B&Bs and small hotels must keep fire detection working and tested under the Fire Safety Order, with weekly user tests and log books under BS 5839-1. Panels sit in 'fault' for weeks (a dead zone or flat battery) and weekly tests go unlogged. Fire authorities prosecute small hotels and B&Bs for exactly these failures, and fines run to tens of thousands.
buyer: Owner-operator of a B&B / guest house / small hotel group
industry: B&Bs, guest houses and small independent hotels
current_workaround: Paper log book, maintainer's 6-monthly visit; ARC monitoring rarely bought by small premises
sensor_concept: Dry contact on the panel's fault/fire relay (or a light sensor over the fault LED) plus a sound sensor that detects the weekly bell test, on LTE-M. Alerts the owner and maintainer on any fault, keeps an automatic weekly test log and produces a monthly compliance report.
notes: c1/c4/c10 strong (RRO prosecutions), c6 BAFE maintainers visit 6-monthly, c8 simple; c7 needs to show ARC is overpriced for small premises; similar duty to the HMO alarm idea but a different buyer.

title: Holiday-let guests overfire wood-burners and set thatch or chimneys alight between annual sweeps
problem: Guests unfamiliar with stoves overfire them with the air wide open, burning wet wood or rubbish. Chimney fires follow, and in thatched cottages the losses run to £100k+. Holiday-let and thatch insurers require regular sweeping (often twice a year for thatch) and certificates, and owners can't see how hard or how often the stove is used.
buyer: Owner-operator or holiday-let agency managing cottages with wood-burners
industry: Self-catering holiday cottages with wood-burning stoves, especially thatched
current_workaround: Sweep once or twice a year regardless of use, laminated stove instructions, stove-pipe thermometers nobody reads
sensor_concept: Thermistor or thermocouple clipped to the flue pipe, on LTE-M. Alerts the owner and guest (SMS) on overfire, logs burn-hours to trigger sweeping by use, and gives sweep and insurer evidence.
notes: c1 thatch fire losses and c4 insurer sweep conditions, c6 HETAS/NACS sweeps visit annually, c8 simple; c2 is seasonal.

title: Holiday parks' scattered fire points lose extinguishers to guests and are checked monthly on foot
problem: Caravan site licence conditions require fire points across the park, and BS 5306-3 expects monthly checks of extinguishers by the responsible person. On parks with hundreds of pitches, extinguishers are stolen, discharged by children or frozen, and staff walk the site monthly. A static caravan fire spreads if the nearest fire point is empty, and the licence and insurer are at risk.
buyer: Park manager / operations director at a holiday park group or independent park
industry: Holiday and touring caravan parks
current_workaround: Monthly on-foot fire-point rounds with paper logs; annual service by the extinguisher contractor
sensor_concept: Presence/tilt sensor on each extinguisher bracket, tamper reed on the cabinet and frost probe for water types, on LoRaWAN with a park gateway. Alerts on removal or tamper, and logs the monthly check automatically.
notes: c2 monthly duty, c3 labour, c4 site licence + BS 5306, c6 extinguisher service firms already visit; c7 versus US en-Gauge (enterprise).

title: Hotel kitchen extract ducts cleaned on a guessed schedule; insurers refuse fire claims when TR19 frequency wasn't met
problem: TR19 sets grease-duct cleaning frequency by daily hours of use (about 3-monthly for heavy use up to 12-monthly for light). Insurers make TR19 compliance a policy condition and have repudiated kitchen-fire claims when cleaning lapsed. Hotels guess their usage band and have no record of real extract hours.
buyer: General manager / chief engineer of an independent or small-group hotel
industry: Hotel kitchens (banqueting/restaurant)
current_workaround: Duct cleaner visits on a fixed contract interval; usage band guessed at the first survey
sensor_concept: Current clamp on the extract fan, on LTE-M. Logs daily run-hours to set the correct TR19 band, alerts when cleaning is due by actual use or the fan fails, and keeps an insurer-ready record.
notes: c1/c4 strong (insurer TR19 conditions + claim refusals), c6 TR19 duct-cleaning contractors visit every 3–12 months, c8 trivial; c7 likely unserved.

title: Holiday parks winterise hundreds of owners' static caravans and get blamed when burst pipes aren't covered
problem: Holiday park operators sell end-of-season winterisation (drain-down) to private caravan owners at ~£100–£150 each, because owners' insurers require drain-down when the park closes. When a missed or partial drain-down bursts pipes, the insurer refuses the claim and the owner blames the park, which brings disputes and refunds.
buyer: Park manager / operations director at a holiday park group
industry: Holiday parks with privately owned static caravans
current_workaround: Paper checklist per caravan, photo of an open drain valve
sensor_concept: Clip-on pipe temperature sensor plus a pulse sensor on the water meter, on LoRaWAN with a park gateway. Proves the system was drained (no flow or pressure) and alerts on frost, giving a per-caravan winterisation certificate.
notes: c5/c6 strong (park sells the service and is on site), c8 simple; c7 risk from the void-property category, so it needs to show the park-level niche is unserved.

title: City hotels' basement sump and sewage pumps fail in storms and flood kitchens and plant rooms
problem: Hotels with basement kitchens, plant rooms and car parks rely on sump and sewage ejector pumps. A failed pump or float during a storm floods the basement (~£50k+ in plant and kitchen damage plus closure). Local panel alarms sound in empty plant rooms, and pump contractors only visit 6-monthly.
buyer: Chief engineer / general manager of a city-centre hotel
industry: Hotels with basement kitchens/plant rooms
current_workaround: Local panel beacon, some legacy GSM diallers, engineer walk-rounds
sensor_concept: Float switch plus current clamp on each pump, on LTE-M. Alerts the engineer and pump contractor on high level, pump failure or abnormal run-time, with a pump-health log.
notes: c1 flood losses and c6 pump service contractors visit; c7 risk from GSM diallers and pump-panel telemetry, and c2 is storm-dependent.
